text:
Priya: Heads-up — ACME reported a sudden spike of 429s and degraded latency this morning after they flipped a proxy change. They say it started ~08:23 UTC.
Devin: Do we have a request ID or example request from them?
Priya: Customer pasted this curl they ran repeatedly: 
```
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-acme-123" \ 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
  -d '{"input":"hello"}' \ 
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
```
They see: `HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests` and header `Retry-After: 5`. No body beyond our standard 429 JSON.
Marta: Any rate-limit headers like X-RateLimit-Remaining/Reset/Limit? Customers often miss them when proxies strip headers.
Priya: They pasted the raw response headers: 
```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Date: Tue, 12 Mar 2025 08:25:01 GMT
Content-Type: application/json
Retry-After: 5
X-Request-ID: req_0a12b3c4
```
No X-RateLimit-* headers.
Devin: Interesting. Lack of X-RateLimit headers usually means the 429 was generated by our edge (IP or proxy) before our app added them, or some middlebox removed them. Could also be IP-based throttling at the gateway.
Marta: Quick checklist: 1) Which auth method used (org key vs project key vs service account)? 2) Are requests coming from a single NATed IP? 3) Any proxy that rewrites/removes headers? 4) Does the API key have project scoped quota?
Priya: They confirmed they're using a shared key (sk-acme-123) that is a project key attached to project "acme-prod". Their infra team said they rolled a new egress NAT in front of everything yesterday to consolidate outbound IPs.
Devin: That points at IP-based quota exhaustion. Our platform has both API-key-scoped and IP-scoped rate limits. If a lot of teammates/services are egressing from the same IP, the IP bucket can fill and start returning 429s without X-RateLimit headers added by the application layer.
Marta: Repro steps we asked them to run to confirm: 1) curl our /v1/keys/{key} (internal admin endpoint) to verify key->project mapping (we provided a sanitized example). 2) Send a request with `X-Forwarded-For: <client-ip>` so we can see if their proxy preserves client IP. 3) Run a quick loop to hit us and capture response headers.
Priya: They ran a loop and sent us one sample trace with headers attached. They also provided server-side logs showing 1000 requests/min coming from a single NAT IP.
Devin: That rate is likely over the IP burst window. We use a token-bucket for IP limiting with a short burst allowance and per-minute refill. If multiple projects share the IP the bucket is shared at the gateway.
Marta: Suggested mitigation to customer: 
- Short-term: rotate to a project-dedicated outbound IP (if cloud provider allows), or spread workers across multiple egress IPs.
- Immediate workaround: create a new project-scoped API key tied to the same project and use that key from fewer hosts — API-key quotas are applied per-key/project and are not affected by other egressing tenants unless IP limit hits first.
Devin: Another quick check for us: confirm whether the gateway that returned 429 is the edge gateway vs upstream rate limiter. I asked infra to grep logs for request id `req_0a12b3c4`.
eli-bot: Incident alert — edge-gateway-1 reported heavy rate-limited responses between 08:20–08:28 UTC. 5xx count unchanged.
Marta: If edge produced the 429, the response may not include X-RateLimit headers. We should still have the internal event with the reason (ip_quota_exhausted or api_key_quota_exhausted).
Priya: They asked whether we can temporarily whitelist the NAT IP while they refactor. Customer urgency: production errors for 30% of traffic.
Devin: We can do a short-term whitelist but need authorization from their account owner and a billing confirmation. Also we should log the change and set an expiration window.
Marta: Long-term fix: recommend they use Dedicated/Reserved capacity or a Dedicated egress pool for high-throughput customers. That will avoid shared IP limits. Also enable per-route batching to reduce QPS.
Priya: I ran a quick account check — their organization shows several active projects. One older project had a runaway job that was recently migrated; looks like it started routing through the same NAT.
Devin: Action items: 
- Priya: get account owner approval for temporary whitelist + duration.
- Devin: find and attach the internal edge log snippet for req_0a12b3c4 and confirm reason code.
- Marta: send customer exact repro steps and suggest the new key + how to check X-RateLimit headers.
Priya: Customer confirmed ok for 2-hour temporary whitelist while they split traffic.
eli-bot: Change request filed: whitelist-nat-54.23.12.9 — expires in 120 minutes — ticket #INC-5492.
Devin: Found edge log: `edge-gw-1 — req_0a12b3c4 — ip_quota_exhausted — nat=54.23.12.9 — rate=1200rpm` (timestamp 08:25:00). Posting the snippet to the ticket.
Marta: For future prevention, recommend they: 
- tag production keys with explicit project labels, so ops can audit which jobs use which key.
- enable per-key QPS caps in console; that lets them throttle at origin before hitting IP limits.
- use SDK with built-in backoff (exponential + jitter) and honor Retry-After.
Priya: I'll update the customer thread with the temporary whitelist details and monitoring steps to verify recovery. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:
Devin: Marking this thread resolved once whitelist expires and we confirm traffic normalized. I'll keep the edge logs attached to the incident ticket.
Marta: Also note — if they ever see 429s with `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` then it was definitely app-level quota; presence/absence of those headers is a good quick heuristics.
Priya: Closing loop with ACME in 30m and will post final status.
